title: Open-ended scenario pattern: collaboratively planned dialogues enacted through off-stage, on-stage, and debriefing phases
description: The open-ended scenario is a pedagogical device designed by DiPietro which resembles a role play in that it grows from a set of circumstances, but differs in that dialogues are planned collaboratively by second-language learners and then acted out. It unfolds in phases: an off-stage phase where the scenario is discussed and planned, an on-stage phase where the dialogue is acted out, and a debriefing stage where interactions and transactions are discussed with the language facilitator. The packet's Part 4 provides guidelines for constructing open-ended scenarios and follow-up procedures.
requirements: A language facilitator leads the debriefing stage in which interactions and transactions are discussed
constraints: The packet presents the scenario device as needing guidelines for construction, provided in Part 4
target_learners: second language learners in K-12 and adult classrooms
target_learning_goals: strategic and interactional competence through authentic language use
examples: Part 4 of the packet covers preparation for open-ended scenario development, guidelines for construction, and follow-up, supported by workshop transparencies and guided discussion items

article_title: Thought Leadership Forum Brief: Talent Development and Opportunity Culture
citation: Center on School Turnaround at WestEd. (2018). Thought Leadership Forum Brief: Talent Development and Opportunity Culture. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://WestEd.org
title: Opportunity Culture defined-role staffing structure (MCLs, MRTs, Elementary Specialists, Team Teachers, Teacher Residents, Reach Associates)
description: Opportunity Culture is "an approach to school design based on a tiered teaching structure within a content area or across one or more grade levels in a school," intended to increase teacher leadership and expand the instructional impact of teachers recognized for strong instruction. Multi-Classroom Leaders lead teacher teams through feedback, coaching, modeling instruction, co-planning, and modeling data analysis, and are accountable for all team student results. Supporting roles include Master Reach Teachers with larger classes aided by technology and interns, Elementary Specialists teaching specific content, Team Teachers, year-long Teacher Residents, and Reach Associates (redesigned paraprofessionals) who supervise students during digital, skills-practice, or project-based learning.
requirements: MCLs must be teachers with excellent instructional practice and adult leadership responsibilities
regular school budgets are repurposed to fund increased pay for leadership roles
constraints: larger class sizes are the norm for Master Reach Teachers, offset by technology, intern teachers, and paraprofessional support
support strategies such as time-technology swaps and remote teaching are adopted in part to offset higher numbers of students
target_learners: K-12 students in turnaround and high-needs schools
target_learning_goals: increase instructional impact of excellent teachers
develop teacher leadership and instructional practice across teams
examples: Charlotte-Mecklenburg's Project LIFT implemented multi-classroom teachers as instructional leaders, elementary specialists, time-technology swaps, and remote teaching across 30 schools
Figure 2 shows seven classroom teacher positions repurposed into an MCL-1, team teachers, a learning coach, a lab monitor, and blended learning teachers using the same funds

citation: Naaz Sibia, Jessica Wen, Amber Richardson, Yashika Jain, Khushi Malik, Bogdan Simion, Carolina Nobre, Angela Zavaleta Bernuy, Andrew Petersen, and Michael Liut. 2026. title: Position visualizations as verification instruments students opt into, with toggleable abstraction levels, rather than as automatically imposed explanation guides
description: The article recommends deploying visualization tools so that learners keep control over when supports appear and how dense they are. The authors state that "friction that learners control can feel productive, while friction that tools impose can feel alienating," and that tools supporting student-chosen reveal timing "may better preserve the sense of active construction that students associate with learning." They further recommend "Toggleable abstraction levels, where students can adjust visual density to their current needs," so one tool can serve students who find metaphors essential and those who find them overwhelming.

constraints: The authors note this does not mean abandoning scaffolding, but designing scaffolds students can opt into rather than having imposed on them
target_learning_goals: preserving active reasoning and engagement with program visualizations
examples: In the study, students who engaged most successfully used the MR tool's views to verify reasoning they had traced manually, and experienced students selectively engaged metaphor views in linked-list tasks despite publicly framing them as beneath them

citation: Alonso-Carracedo, M., Fernandez-Boullon, R., Celard, P., Rodríguez-Martínez, F. J., & Otero-Cerdeira, L. (2026). CogTax: A Four-Level Cognitive Taxonomy for Command-Line Computing Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00140
title: Sequence command-line instruction so operational safety is established before operational power, consolidating each level's prerequisites before the next
description: The article derives a constructivist curriculum sequencing principle from the taxonomy: each level's prerequisites should be fully consolidated before the next level is introduced, with course units introducing L(k+1) material assuming mastery of all L1...L(k) concepts. It states that "The L= max(C, O) decomposition has a specific implication for introductory courses: operational safety should be established before operational power is introduced." Worked examples should be provided at the ZPD boundary, with the two dimensions separated where possible, introducing conceptually complex but operationally safe commands before operationally impactful ones.
requirements: An explicit ordered complexity taxonomy so material can be placed relative to each learner's current competence; grounding in constructivist scaffolding and Cognitive Load Theory
constraints: Grounded in command-line computing education; the article notes cognitive patterns of some L3 commands (e.g., pipelines) may be conceptually accessible earlier than their operational impact allows
target_learners: undergraduate students learning Linux system administration
target_learning_goals: safe progression from read-only inspection to advanced system management operations

citation: Ye, P.-G., Mo, K., Long, Y., Liu, M., Sang, H., & Zheng, J. (2026). ARPG+: a simulation-based study of real-time coaching for educational LLM prompting. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00606-9
title: Operationalizing cognitive load theory and ZPD into real-time coaching signals
description: The article transforms cognitive load theory and zone of proximal development into "calibratable, real-time signals": an overload-risk estimator grounded in intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load proxies; a normalized Struggle Index quantifying interactional friction from editing and pausing behaviors; and an uncertainty-aware ability tracker maintaining dynamic ZPD boundaries. ZPD is represented as a time-varying band [µt − κσt, µt + κσt] compared against estimated task demand.

constraints: All computations are validated only on LLM-based simulated learners; the authors state this does not constitute empirical validation with real students.

target_learning_goals: Prompting skill development

title: Operational definition of emerging technologies in TEFL: novel, rapidly adopted tools and pedagogical approaches aligned with SLA theory, with context-dependent and temporally dynamic emerging status
description: The review synthesizes prior definitions (Veletsianos, 2010; Rotolo et al., 2015; the New Media Consortium's one-to-five-year horizon) into an operational definition: "Emerging technologies in TEFL are innovative tools, platforms, or pedagogical approaches that have the potential to significantly transform language teaching and learning practices." potential for enhancing authentic communication and cultural understanding

title: Opportunity structures for belonging: interpersonal, instructional, and institutional pathways from racial climate to belonging
description: The article adopts Gray et al.'s (2018, 2020) construct of opportunity structures for belonging, defined as "aspects of a school or classroom environment that fulfill or thwart students' needs to belong." title: Time-penalty grading rules separating easy and hard opposites into ranked credit classes
description: The authors propose a standardized grading scheme in which errors and omissions are converted into added seconds: for easy opposites "The penalty for an omitted word was four seconds", with exact opposites given full credit and a second class given one-half credit; for hard opposites an omitted or entirely wrong word drew an eighteen-second penalty, with intermediate response classes ranked at two-thirds and one-third value. target_learning_goals: controlled association (easy opposites) and logical keenness in selecting contrary ideas (hard opposites)

citation: Silver, A. M., Elliott, L., & Libertus, M. E. (2022). Parental math input is not uniformly beneficial for young children: The moderating role of inhibitory control. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000679
title: Opportunity-Propensity framework extended: opportunity and propensity factors interact to shape children's achievement
description: The Opportunity-Propensity framework explains children's development by the learning opportunities provided in the environment and children's propensity to learn, including antecedent factors like socioeconomic status. This article notes the framework "has typically employed mediational path modeling" treating opportunity and propensity as independent predictors, and extends it by showing the two interact: children's inhibitory control (propensity) determines whether parental number talk (opportunity) relates to math achievement. The authors state that "opportunities and propensities interact to shape children's performance rather than independently predicting math achievement."
requirements: Requires measuring both an environmental opportunity factor and a child-level propensity factor in the same sample, and testing their interaction rather than only main effects.
constraints: Evidence in this article is concurrent and correlational, drawn from a predominantly White, highly educated sample, so the authors caution the findings "may not extend to other populations in other contexts" and causal conclusions cannot be drawn.

examples: Regressing TEMA-3 math scores on parent number talk, child inhibitory control, and their interaction while controlling for overall talk, parent math achievement, vocabulary, age, and gender.

description: The article's conceptual framework organises early-adopter practice into six categories: Characteristics for Learning, Teaching Approach, Open Data in Society, Creating and Sharing, Skills and Knowledge, and Making Data Usable. It was derived from thematic analysis of ten educator interviews, in which "The final refined analysis described below has 6 categories that contain 28 themes". The framework maps perceived strengths of open data, activity designs, societal interactions, collaborative practices, literacy requirements, and the preparation work needed for learning activities, and is offered to support greater use of open data by educators.
requirements: Educators need awareness of open data and its distinction from other online content, which the article reports is currently lacking among educators.
constraints: The framework was built from a purposive sample of ten early adopters in a specialised area and descriptive analysis, not from controlled comparison.
target_learners: Educators and teachers across school, college, university, MOOC and skills-training contexts
target_learning_goals: Data literacies, subject-matter learning, critical thinking, and public engagement with open data
examples: Communicating with data was identified by all ten interviewees as a key skill, with storytelling roles embedded in teaching materials.
key_sources: Tim Coughlan. (2020). The use of open data as a material for learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09706-y

article_title: Approaches to illuminate content-specific gameplay decisions using open-ended game data
citation: Rosenheck, Louisa; Cheng, Meng-Tzu; Lin, Chen-Yen; Klopfer, Eric. (2021). Approaches to illuminate content-specific gameplay decisions using open-ended game data. Springer US. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09989-0
title: Design learning games with open-ended tasks and granular log data to elicit evidence of thinking
description: The article states that illuminating content-specific gameplay decisions "requires a context that is open-ended enough for students to make choices that demonstrate their thinking" and also "requires rich log data and methods of Game Learning Analytics (GLA) that are granular enough to look at the specific choices most relevant to that context and domain". Designers should therefore pair open-ended task structures with fine-grained analytics targeted at domain-relevant choices.
requirements: Open-ended game context permitting meaningful choices
Rich log data and granular GLA methods matched to the domain
constraints: Granularity must be matched to the specific context and domain of interest
target_learning_goals: Demonstrating conceptual understanding and inquiry processes through gameplay choices
examples: The Radix Endeavor quest on Mendelian genetics served as the open-ended context with log data analyzed at the level of specific choices

article_title: Educators' open educational collaboration online: The dilemma of emotional ownership
citation: Educators' Open Educational Collaboration Online: The Dilemma of Emotional Ownership. (2016). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1115784
title: Model of educators' intention to engage in open educational collaboration in virtual communities
description: The article validates a data-driven model explaining educators' behavioral intention to engage in open educational collaboration in virtual communities. It comprises seven personal-level influencing factors — intention (INTOE), emotional ownership (OWN), outcome expectations (OE), preference for exchanging ideas online (PEI), affective community commitment (ACC), previous experience (EXP), and preference for collaborative OER development (ENJ) — plus two organizational control variables. The model was tested with structural equation modelling on survey data from 100 educators.
requirements: Survey measurement of all constructs using adapted or newly developed scales validated through exploratory factor analysis
constraints: Organizational innovativeness and OER awareness control paths showed no significant effects
target_learners: educators in higher education and other educational institutions
target_learning_goals: collaborative development of open educational resources and practices

description: The authors made the meta-analysis RLOs freely and openly accessible under a Creative Commons licence on the University of Nottingham SONET website. One reason was "the difficulties students had accessing materials requiring usernames and passwords and remembering to access them". The conclusions state that openly accessible RLOs "provide flexible support for students who find the process of meta-analysis difficult".

article_title: Findings from a Multi-Year Scale-Up Effectiveness Trial of Open-Court Reading (Imagine It!)
citation: Vaden-Kiernan, M., Borman, G., Caverly, S., Bell, N., Ruiz de Castilla, V., Sullivan, K., & Fleming, G. (2016). Findings from a Multi-Year Scale-Up Effectiveness Trial of Open-Court Reading (Imagine It!). SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Open Court Reading (Imagine It!) phonics-based K-6 core reading curriculum
description: The Open Court Reading (OCR) program, published by SRA/McGraw-Hill and widely used since the 1960s, is a phonics-based core reading curriculum for kindergarten through 6th grade that "incorporates many of the instructional practices related to phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and text comprehension recommended by the National Reading Panel (2000)". The curriculum includes student materials, teacher manuals, diagnostic and assessment tools, and test preparation practice guides, with a 2- or 3-day summer workshop and ongoing support from OCR reading consultants. In all grades the instructional format is a three-part lesson covering vocabulary, comprehension strategies, and comprehension skills, with informal and formal assessments used to monitor progress and inform instruction.
requirements: Teacher training via a 2- or 3-day summer workshop on program implementation plus ongoing school-year support from OCR reading consultants
target_learners: elementary school students in kindergarten through 5th grade
target_learning_goals: reading proficiency, including phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and text comprehension
examples: Evaluated at scale in a multi-site cluster randomized trial of 49 elementary schools in 7 districts, with schools randomly assigned to treatment (N=25) and comparison (N=24) blocking at the district level.

article_title: Animation Model to Conceptualize ATP Generation: A Mitochondrial Oxidative Phosphorylation
citation: Jena, A. K. (2015). Animation model to conceptualize ATP generation: A study of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 3(1), 61-76. https://scholar.google.com
title: Oxidative Phosphorylation Concept Test (OPCT), a 15-item multiple-choice misconception test
description: The OPCT is a fifteen-item multiple-choice misconception test on ATP synthesis and the chemiosmotic hypothesis, each item having "one correct answer and two powerful distracters" designed to diagnose misconception types. It was developed through a table of specifications, expert review, and primary, secondary, and final tryouts, with content validity ratio CVR = .68 and Cronbach Alpha reliability 0.76. The same test served as pretest (misconception test) and posttest for both groups, with a maximum of twenty minutes to respond.
requirements: Items prepared with equal difficulty and discrimination power, reviewed by experts of life science, science education, and measurement and evaluation
constraints: Evaluated by three biology teachers having more than 5 years teaching experience in biology
target_learning_goals: understanding of ATP generation by mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and diagnosis of associated misconceptions
examples: Administered to both groups as pretest and posttest; items 1, 5, 8, 10, and 14 were identified as preconceived notion type misconceptions

title: Open-ended performance-based assessment tests for senior high school mathematics
description: Two equivalent performance-based assessment tests were developed for individual completion, with items built from selected syllabus topics and answers developed with assessment and mathematics experts. Reliability estimates for pre-test and post-test were "0.67 and 0.70, respectively, using K-R 20 formula", and content validity was established by matching test questions to specific syllabus objectives. Answers developed with the help of assessment and mathematics experts

article_title: Cluster Randomized Trial of a Large-Scale Education Initiative in the Democratic Republic of Congo: Pilot Year Impacts on Teacher Development
citation: Wolf, S., Aber, J. L., Torrente, C., Rasheed, D., & McCoy, M. (2014). Cluster randomized trial of a large-scale education initiative in the Democratic Republic of Congo: Pilot year impacts on teacher development. SREE Spring 2014 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: OPEQ: integrated reading and math curriculum with Healing Classrooms techniques plus school-based collaborative professional development through Forums of Pedagogical Exchange

It combines an innovative curriculum integrating reading and math lessons with IRC's Healing Classrooms techniques "to create safe and inclusive learning environments for all learners", and a school-based collaborative professional development system built on the DRC tradition of Forums of Pedagogical Exchange, delivered by Master Trainers, one per cluster of 2 to 6 schools.
requirements: Delivery relies on Master Trainers drawn from teachers, headmasters, pedagogical advisors, inspectors and Ministry of Education technical staff, one per cluster of 2 to 6 schools

elementary school children in Katanga, DRC

children's numeracy, literacy and socio-emotional wellbeing

article_title: The Effects of the Computer-Based Instruction on the Achievement and Problem Solving Skills of the Science and Technology Students
citation: Serin, O. (2011). The effects of the computer-based instruction on the achievements and problem solving skills of the science and technology students. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Graded-step, feedback-rich self-paced computerized instruction grounded in operant conditioning
description: The study's materials follow Skinner's operant conditioning: content is broken into graded steps, learners stay active, and correct responses are reinforced immediately. As the article states, "The materials and activities are presented in graded steps. Learners have the opportunity to be active in the learning process and receive immediate feedback and work at their own pace." In the software this appears as congratulatory audio and smiling faces for correct answers, required correct answers before advancing, and clue pages for errors.
requirements: Immediate feedback on answers and self-pacing are required features; tutorial developers are said to incorporate the principle of practice and reinforcement.
constraints: The article ties this pattern mainly to drill-and-practice and tutorial modes of computerized learning.
target_learning_goals: science concept learning
meaningful rather than rote learning
examples: In the 'Shall we exercise?' section a correct answer triggered 'Congratulations! You can pass on to the next question' with a smiling face; wrong answers brought up a clue page the pupil could take.

article_title: From a Gloss to a Learning Tool: Does Visual Aids Enhance Better Sentence Comprehension?
citation: Takeshi Sato and Akio Suzuki. (2012). From a Gloss to a Learning Tool: Does Visual Aids Enhance Better Sentence Comprehension? EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. https://research-publishing.net
title: Optimize visual glosses according to the learning target rather than assuming technologically advanced glosses are better
description: The article argues that glosses in CALL should be treated as learning tools rather than mere reference glosses, and that the choice of visual gloss configuration should be optimized to the target vocabulary. As the authors put it, "optimization of the glosses according to the target should be required." The principle rests on their finding that animated stereo images offered no advantage over planar still images.
requirements: Attention to the meaning structures of the target words, such as part of speech and sense structure, when selecting gloss types
constraints: The article states this result does not mean using technology or multimedia functions has no meaning; further research is needed
target_learners: L2 learners of English, such as Japanese university students
target_learning_goals: Learning the senses of polysemous English spatial prepositions
examples: The study compared planar still images and animated stereo images depicting conceptual schemes of English spatial prepositions in a ten-minute intentional learning session

article_title: How Do Openers Contribute to Student Learning?
citation: Zertuche, A., Gerard, L., & Linn, M. C. (2012). How do Openers Contribute to Student Learning? International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 5(1), 79-92. http://www.iejee.com
title: Design Openers that are non-evaluative, soon after topic introduction, evidence-based, and short
description: The article distills four design principles for Openers in technology-enhanced instruction: Openers "can reinforce normative conceptual ideas by drawing attention to the distinction between student ideas and normative views"; they help when they occur soon after a topic is introduced and direct attention to specific improvements; they succeed when non-evaluative and supportive of exploring peer evidence; and they should be short, with student review of examples possibly moved to homework.
requirements: Easy access to evidence of students' ideas and efficient routines to elicit students' ideas during class
constraints: The Openers in this study were much longer and had more teacher involvement than recommended; the voting process did not work as anticipated in some classes
target_learning_goals: Revising and refining scientific explanations of chemical reactions
examples: Teachers used the WISE flag tool to select student work examples illustrating conceptual errors for whole-class critique during the Opener.

article_title: Towards a Practical Framework of the Remediation of Cognitive Skills at Primary Level
citation: Outi Kyrö-Ämmälä & Kaarina Määttä. (2011). Towards a Practical Framework of the Remediation of Cognitive Skills at Primary Level. World Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v1n1p28
title: Discuss mistakes openly in a trusting classroom climate so every pupil learns from them
description: In the remedial teaching method, which is interactive and dialogical, pupils must be able to work independently in a confidential atmosphere. The article argues that "By developing a teaching group's togetherness, also the mistakes can ope nly be discussed without a fear for a single pupil who made a mistake would be made fun of". The teacher highlights mistakes, discusses alternative solution methods and common misunderstandings before too many pupils make them, and dissects even a single pupil's mistake with the whole class so everyone can learn from every mistake.

target_learners: primary-level pupils, including those afraid of making mistakes

understanding alternative solution methods
examples: The teacher guides the lesson carefully and watches closely every pupil's development all the time

examples: The pretest was administered after group selection to ensure the three groups were equally proficient before the eight-week treatment

article_title: The Effects of Explicit and Implicit Pragmatic Instruction on the Development of Compliments and Compliment Responses
citation: Saman Ebadi, Mahsa Pourzandi. (2015). The Effects of Explicit and Implicit Pragmatic Instruction on the Development of Compliments and Compliment Responses. li-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 5, No. 4, October - December. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=The+Effects+of+Explicit+and+Implicit+Pragmatic+Instruction+on+the+Development+of+Compliments+and+Compliment+Responses
title: Open-ended Discourse Completion Test (DCT) with 12 compliment situations
description: The study's primary instrument is an open-ended Discourse Completion Test adopted from Chen and Boonkongsaen's (2012) study, which took its 12 situations from Yuan (2002). examples: Item one of part one asked learners to compliment a classmate helping a charity; item one of part two asked them to respond to an explicit compliment about their appearance

citation: Goodridge, W. H., Lawanto, O., & Santoso, H. B. (2017). A Learning Style Comparison between Synchronous Online and Face-to-Face Engineering Graphics Instruction. International Education Studies, 10(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n2p1
title: Open-ended ill-structured capstone design project as the culminating activity in an engineering graphics course
description: The course culminated in "an open ended, ill structured final design project as a capstone activity" worth 25% of the grade: a robotic arm in solid modeling software capable of picking up a ping pong ball and a pencil. Students worked in teams of two over 4 weeks, dividing arm and gripper components, encouraged to think economically about cost and materials within a given work envelope. Solutions were analyzed for adherence to size and economy constraints and demonstrated via animation.
requirements: Solid Edge solid modeling software, team pairs, a 4-week design window, and a defined work envelope with size and economy constraints
constraints: The work envelope was set to given dimensions simulating constraints that often exist in engineering

examples: Students designed a robotic gripper versatile enough to handle two objects without changing the mechanism, verified part interaction on completed assembly models, and submitted dimensioned multi-view drawings, an isometric drawing, jpeg files, and design journal entries

Collaboration and interaction among stakeholders including the community
constraints: Requires validation both in conceptual and practical ways

collaboration
peer-partnership

title: Opioid Room of Horrors: an error-driven simulation with four errors and four hazards for safe opioid administration training
description: The opioid Room of Horrors is a 30-minute paired simulation in which healthcare professionals prepare and administer an opioid to a fictitious geriatric patient in a realistic room with a mannequin, mock electronic medical record, medicine cabinet and nurse trolley. The room hides four errors and four hazards covering steps of the opioid medication-use process, which participants must detect or avoid; assessors then debrief with feedback and a refresh of the 5R rule and the double-check process. Performing an independent double-check
Detecting medication administration errors and avoiding hazards in the opioid medication-use process

description: A methodological framework in which robotic-platform OPIs are binned by month, reduced with t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding, and compared across consecutive time bins using "Euclidean distance between consecutive bins" weighted by days elapsed and case volume, then smoothed. article_title: The grass isn't always greener: perceptions of and performance on open-note exams.
citation: Sato, B. K., He, W., Warschauer, M., & Kadandale, P. (2015). The Grass Isn't Always Greener: Perceptions of and Performance on Open-Note Exams. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.14-08-0121
title: When introducing open-note testing, explain its rationale and align assessment objectives with higher-order question design
description: The article's authors distill practical considerations for instructors adopting open-note exams: explain why the format is being introduced, and ensure the exam's questions match its stated objectives. They stress that "there must not be a dissonance between the stated objectives of the assessment and the kinds of questions used in the assessment" — telling students data analysis matters while writing mostly lower-Bloom's questions sends a mixed message. They argue open-note testing pushes instructors toward higher-order exams.
requirements: Instructors must explain why open-note testing is being introduced, stressing that success requires independent analysis of data rather than recitation of the author's text.
Assessment objectives and the kinds of questions used must be aligned, with exams emphasizing higher-order Bloom's levels rather than memorization.
constraints: The study found no overall performance benefit of open-note testing, and the authors state that increased frequency of open-note testing in a curriculum may be necessary before firm conclusions about the intervention can be drawn.
target_learners: undergraduate biology students in large-enrollment laboratory courses
target_learning_goals: critical thinking and critical analysis of primary literature
higher-order thinking on Bloom's levels 3–6
examples: In the study's courses, instructors told students the paper quiz would focus on understanding the scientific article and analyzing figures rather than memorizing background material or the authors' conclusions.

description: OpenMeta[Analyst] is described as "a free downloadable meta-analysis program" used in the course to teach synthesis and heterogeneity interpretation.
